candidates.title: Ajar: Measuring Open Privilege in Agent Defenses
candidates.summary: A language model agent acts through the tools it is given. The data it reads while working on a task can redirect what it does with those tools. A growing set of techniques for safe and secure agent execution therefore sits between the agent and its tools, aiming to enforce access control, information flow or isolation at that boundary. candidates.title: Silent Failures in Agentic Security Evaluation: A Validated Harness for Tool-Call Mediation Under Indirect Prompt Injection
candidates.summary: LLM agents that invoke privileged tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved data hijack the agent's actions. A growing body of work evaluates defenses against IPI, but the validity of that evaluation is rarely examined. We audit an IPI benchmark and its harness and identify four defect classes -- silent payload non-delivery, attack success scored by tool identity rather than arguments, false-rejection rate conflated with model incapacity, and the absence of an audit trail -- each of which yields a plausible, publishable, and incorrect number. candidates.title: The Security Duality of Large Language Model Agents: A Systematic Review of Self-Security Protection and Cybersecurity Empowerment
candidates.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents integrate memory, tool invocation, environment interaction, and multi-agent collaboration, evolving from passive text-generation tools into autonomous systems that execute complex tasks. This capability leap creates a pronounced security duality. On the one hand, LLM agents face emerging threats such as jailbreak attacks, prompt injection, memory poisoning, and multi-agent collusion, requiring systematic self-security protection. candidates.title: CoER: Defending against Adaptive Indirect Prompt Injection via Adversarial Co-Evolution and Refinement
candidates.summary: Language-model agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) during tool use: adversarial instructions hidden in untrusted tool outputs can covertly redirect legitimate task execution. Existing work often trains and evaluates defenses against fixed attacks that do not adapt to the defender's behavior, so the resulting defenses may struggle against adaptive attacks in real-world settings. We argue that a strong defense against adaptive IPI must adapt during training to a continually evolving attacker. candidates.title: CounterSteer: Suppressing Indirect Prompt Injection with Activation Steering
candidates.summary: Indirect prompt injection makes an LLM agent treat untrusted retrieved text as instructions. We present CounterSteer, an inference-time defense that suppresses this behavior inside the model. Per model, a five-step recipe fits a residual-stream direction from paired episodes differing only in whether an embedded instruction is followed, and retains it only if it passes pre-specified causal and capability gates. At deployment, the direction is subtracted from every tool-result token during prefill. candidates.title: Mitigating Direct and Indirect Prompt Injection in Production LLM Agents: A Defense-in-Depth Architectural Framework and Empirical Benchmark
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.summary: Building software systems around Large Language Model (LLM) agents introduces a hard security problem: how to prevent untrusted inputs from hijacking tool calls and database queries. While jailbreaks in conversational chats are well documented, indirect prompt injections—malicious payloads embedded in database rows, web pages, or customer feedback—threaten production pipelines. In this technical note, we evaluate why relying on system prompts alone fails under practical evasion techniques. candidates.title: SafeAgent: Dual-Objective Optimization Against Prompt and Tool Injection in Interactive Environments
candidates.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents that interact with external tools, web content, and code repositories face significant security risks from prompt injection and tool manipulation attacks. However, overly restrictive security measures often render agents ineffective, creating a fundamental tension between safety and utility. We propose SafeAgent, a dual-objective optimization framework that simultaneously quantifies and balances these competing goals. candidates.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents turn credential hygiene from a storage problem into an execution-security problem. candidates.title: CoDeL: Co-Evolutionary Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM-based Agents
candidates.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on external tools and content, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI). This threat has motivated a wide range of defenses, among which training-based defenses are often regarded as most reliable. However, existing training-based defenses are typically optimized on a static distribution of explicit injections. They learn surface-form cues rather than the boundary between serving the user and obeying an injected objective, and therefore fail when malicious intent is folded into a plausible workflow and deferred for several turns. candidates.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving from chat interfaces into infrastructure operations, where they read telemetry, call tools, generate and execute code, and change the state of production Kubernetes clusters. candidates.summary: Agent interaction protocols such as ACP and A2A have moved LLM-based agents toward multi-agent collaboration, introducing new security threats. candidates.summary: Large language model email assistants are particularly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection because untrusted email content can be retrieved into the model context and influence subsequent tool use. candidates.title: The Verifiable Action Card: Trustworthy Human-in-the-Loop Control for Secure Autonomous Agents
candidates.summary: Agentic browsers can execute security-sensitive actions under a user's authenticated session, making indirect prompt injection and deceptive confirmation interfaces a direct threat to action integrity. candidates.title: Authority Is Not a String: A Capability-Scoped Harness for Prompt-Injection-Resistant Coding Agents
candidates.summary: Coding agents use system-level tools to read files, execute commands, and modify source code. Within the agent’s sandbox, these tools often carry ambient authority: naming a resource is sufficient to act on it. Indirect prompt injection exploits this authority by placing instructions in repository files or tool output that cause the agent to perform actions the user did not request.

candidates.title: Certified Multi-Source Integrity for Structured Agent Actions
candidates.summary: LLM agents increasingly take privileged, often irreversible structured actions, such as paying an invoice. Current defenses gate on a source's trust label or certify free-text answer quality. None certifies the integrity of a coupled, policy-bound structured action under a corruption budget that accounts for shared upstream sources. candidates.title: Same Bytes, Different Authority: Reserved-Token Representations in Chat-Template Prompt Injection
candidates.summary: Prompt injection against LLM agents becomes much stronger when the injected instruction is wrapped in the model's own chat template. We use this to measure how much of the injected instruction's authority comes from the reserved token's learned representation.
